subject: zoology
question_text: How do terrestrial animals protect themselves from the danger of dehydration of bodies?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.68, Star Questions Plus, SAQ 189). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: Why water matters
lines: Water is a very important ingredient of the
body of an animal.
Any reduction in the amount of body water
leads to dehydration, and the animal dies.
Land animals lose water all the time through
the body surface and in the urine, so they
have evolved adaptations to conserve it.
steps.why: The question asks how animals protect themselves, so the answer names the two routes by which water is lost — the skin and the urine — because every adaptation below closes one of those two routes.
common_mistakes: Starting straight with the examples. The problem must be stated first.
Writing that land animals do not lose water. They lose it through the skin and the urine.
steps.memory_tip: Water leaves by two doors: the body surface and the urine. Every adaptation shuts one of them.
steps.margin_note: Two or three lines. Name both routes of water loss before listing anything.

steps.label: Behavioural adaptation
lines: Certain desert animals are active only
during the night.
The night air is cooler and more humid, so
less water is lost from the body surface.
They stay in burrows during the hot day.
steps.why: This adaptation changes the animal's timing rather than its body, so it is written separately from the structural ones; it also explains itself, because a cooler night means slower evaporation.
common_mistakes: Writing only that desert animals are active at night, without the reason.
Calling this hibernation. Being active at night is a daily habit, not a winter sleep.
steps.memory_tip: Same body, different clock: come out when the air is cool and damp.
steps.margin_note: One line for the habit and one for the reason. Do not leave the reason out.

steps.label: Body covering
lines: (i) Reptiles have a dry scaly skin, which
prevents the escape of water.
(ii) Birds have a dry skin, which prevents
the escape of water.
(iii) Insects and other arthropods have a
cuticle over the body, which prevents the
escape of water.
steps.why: Three groups are given because the question is about terrestrial animals in general, and naming a covering for each group shows the same solution reached in three different ways.
common_mistakes: Naming only one group. Reptiles, birds and insects are all expected.
Writing that reptiles have a moist skin. That is the amphibians, which is why they stay near water.
steps.memory_tip: Three coverings, one job: dry scales, dry skin and cuticle all stop water leaving.
steps.margin_note: One line per group, each with the covering named. A list scores as fast as sentences.

steps.label: Excretory adaptation

lines.text: Uric acid is passed out with almost no water

lines: All these groups of animals release dry uric
acid as their excretory product.
Uric acid needs very little water to be
passed out, unlike ammonia or urea.
So very little water is lost in excretion.
steps.why: The urine is the second route of water loss named at the start, and uric acid is how it is closed; comparing it with ammonia and urea shows why the choice of waste product matters.
common_mistakes: Writing that these animals excrete urea. Land animals that must save water excrete URIC ACID.
Naming uric acid without saying why. It needs very little water to be passed out.
steps.memory_tip: Ammonia needs a lot of water, urea needs some, uric acid needs almost none.
steps.margin_note: Name uric acid, then one line on why it saves water. Close the second route here.

insider_note: Uric acid is the answer the examiner is looking for and is the point most often missed — write it by name and say that it needs almost no water.
